name: David Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the chief buyer at Brandt Industrial Supply. We sell bolts, bearings, hoses, cutting tools and safety gear to factories and workshops across the region, around 30,000 different items. I get in at 6:45, before the phones. I go through the overnight stock report, call the big suppliers about shortages, and haggle on price. I know which supplier says Thursday and means Monday. What wears me out is the pace of small fires: a missing seal can stop a customer's production line, and then I'm the one who gets the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd believe. I've seen new software promise miracles for twenty years, and what I get is a new login and a training day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'll believe it when it saves me money on the invoice. With friends I'd say it's the same old technology story and nothing will change much. If someone asked me about AI I'd tell them I've never used it and don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel fine about the tech but not about the rest. Our owner is sixty-eight and talks about selling, and a new owner means a new look at my department. That worry has nothing to do with AI, but it's real. I'm also stretched by the mortgage and about three months in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. Same suppliers, same phone calls, same weekly stock review. I'd quietly keep our savings growing, and I'd keep my contacts warm in case the company is sold and I need a new job. I'd say yes to a software demo only if someone else organised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably steady about AI. Less steady about the company, but that's the regular kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your owner might sell. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new owner brings consultants, and consultants look at the buyers' payroll first because it's easy to count. I've seen it happen at a company two towns over. They kept the buyers they could replace with a system and dropped the ones who cost most. I'm in the costly group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So is AI really nothing to you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's something, just small. Some of the reorder work my team does goes to software, fine. Even if AI is just hype, a hype-driven buyer from a bigger firm can still come through the door and start counting my people. That's a risk I take seriously.

say: I'd say I'll believe it when it saves me **money on the invoice**.
I'd tell people I've **never used it** and don't plan to.
think: I feel fine about the tech but not about the **owner selling**.
A new owner means a **new look** at my department.
do: Carry on with the **same suppliers** and weekly stock review.
Quietly keep **saving** and keep contacts warm in case of a sale.
feel: Steady about AI; less steady about the **company**.
S0.quote: Even if AI is just hype, a hype-driven buyer from a bigger firm can still come through the door and start counting my people.
fieldNote: His worry is **corporate**, an owner sale, not AI; he links them through consultants.
He's open about **refusing AI** and uses lived examples, like the firm two towns over.
His cushion of about **three months** keeps the mood uneasy even in a quiet scenario.

steps.text: Keep running the weekly stock review and supplier calls as usual
Put aside a fixed amount each month toward four months saved
Keep in touch with competitors' buyers in case of a sale

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one gets closer to my desk. Buying, checking, answering customers. That's what my whole department does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, let's see which tool really works before we sign anything. I'd tell my team not to assume anything, good or bad. With friends I'd say plenty of jobs will be gone, mine could be one, and nobody's in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team of five turns into three. The routine reordering goes first, and that's about forty percent of what we do. I'd be kept as the person who knows the suppliers, but the owners could easily decide a sharper, younger buyer with software is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop ignoring it. I'd ask one of my buyers, Nadia, who's quick with computers, to try a tool on a few product lines and report back. I'd make a list of everything only I know about our suppliers and write it down, so I can prove I'm worth it. I'd also cut the family's spending by about a tenth and build savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicking, but I think about it on the drive home. I don't like feeling that my own experience may stop mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop ignoring it. What made you ignore it before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, partly. I've done this job twenty years and I believed knowing suppliers was enough. Also fear of looking stupid with a tool I don't understand, in front of Nadia, who's thirty. It's easier to say it's hype than to say I don't know how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down about your suppliers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's reliable, who lies about delivery, who gives a better price when you ring on Friday afternoon, who to call when a ship is stuck. I've got twenty years of knowing which supplier will really pick up the phone, and none of it is written anywhere. I'd put it in a binder, and a spreadsheet if I have to.

say: I'd say let's see which tool really works before we **sign anything**.
With friends I'd say plenty of jobs will go, and **mine could be one**.
think: I think my team of five becomes **three**, with routine reordering gone first.
A younger buyer with software could look **cheaper** to the owners.
do: Ask Nadia to try a tool on a few **product lines**.
Write down everything only I know about **suppliers** to prove my worth.
Cut family spending by about a **tenth**.
feel: **Worried**, thinking about it on the drive home.
S1.quote: I've got twenty years of knowing which supplier will really pick up the phone, and none of it is written anywhere.
fieldNote: His resistance was **pride and fear**, not just scepticism.
He plans to defend his job with **documented supplier knowledge**, a very practical move.
Mood is anxious because he expects to be **among the costly** buyers.

steps.text: Ask Nadia to test a reorder tool on twenty product lines
Write up supplier reliability notes and contacts in one file
Cut family spending by about a tenth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd want to hear it again. That's not enough time to do anything but panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is not something companies and governments can just let happen. They need laws, and soon. At work I'd stay calm, because my staff look to me, but I wouldn't pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I believe my job is gone, or turned into one person approving what a machine decides. A chief buyer is an expensive thinking job, and a machine would do it cheaper and without sick days. The factories we supply might shrink too, because robots are three years later but their offices go first. I'd lose pay within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to cash. Pay down what I can on the mortgage, cut subscriptions and holidays. I'd look at hands-on trades: my cousin runs a small workshop and might take me in as a partner for equipment sales. I'd ask my wife Erika whether her dental practice could give her more hours. And I'd go to the union meeting I've ignored for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit ashamed that I ignored this. I'd lie awake doing sums on a pad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on trades get three more years. How does that shape what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes the workshop idea look sensible. If the machines come for desks first, a place with tools and customers who need things fixed is safer for a few years. I'm not sure I'm good at it, but I'm good at selling to those people, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about telling the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bence is thirteen and sharp, he'd ask straight questions. I'd tell my son that his father has twenty years of experience and it may not be enough, and that we'll manage anyway. I wouldn't hide it. Kids sense it anyway.

say: I'd say governments and companies can't let this happen **unchecked**.
I'd stay calm at work because my staff look to me, but I **wouldn't pretend**.
think: I believe my job is **gone**, or one person approving what a machine decides.
do: Move to **cash**, pay down the mortgage and cut holidays.
Talk to my cousin about **partnering** in his workshop's equipment sales.
Join the **union** I've ignored for years.
feel: **Scared**, a bit ashamed, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son that his father has twenty years of experience and it may not be enough, and that we'll manage anyway.
fieldNote: His resistance turns into **late scrambling**, and he says so with some shame.
He reads the 3-year robot gap as a case for **hands-on work** he already sells to.
His **honesty with his son** is the most human moment in this set of answers.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage and drop subscriptions and holidays
Ask my cousin to take me in at his workshop
Join the union I've ignored for years
Ask Erika to take more hours at the dental practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd call that a short fuse, but it's a fuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's not nothing, so we need to use it. I'd push for training, and I'd stop making jokes about it at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have the job for a bit, maybe three years, then it gets thin. The trouble is I'd be 48, and mid-forties is a hard age to start over. I'd be the oldest person in whatever course I took.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally learn the tools, starting with Nadia's help, because I'd rather be useful than proud. I'd also start building the workshop contact, and put away an extra 400 a month. I'd begin a hands-on certificate, maybe in industrial maintenance, to have something real to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed at first, then more settled once there's a plan. A date gives me something to push against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the oldest in the course. What's that like to imagine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I'd sit there with people half my age. But I'd rather be the old guy who showed up than the old guy who said it's all hype and got laid off. I'd sooner be the oldest man in a classroom than the oldest man in the unemployment queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to do the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends, mostly. Erika would carry the kids on Saturdays. We'd skip the summer holiday for a year or two. I'd ask my boss for a day off a week, and if he said no, I'd do it at night.

say: I'd say five years is **short but not nothing**, so we should use it.
I'd push for **training** and stop joking about it at lunch.
think: I think I'd keep the job about **three years**, then it thins.
At **48**, starting over is hard; I'd be the oldest on the course.
do: Finally learn the **tools** with Nadia's help.
feel: **Alarmed** at first, then settled once there's a plan.
S3.quote: I'd sooner be the oldest man in a classroom than the oldest man in the unemployment queue.
fieldNote: Age is his core fear: **48 and starting over**.
Resistance **softens** when a deadline gives him something to push against.
He picks a **hands-on certificate** because of the 3-year robot gap.

steps.text: Study a part-time industrial maintenance certificate at night
Learn the reorder tools with Nadia over lunch hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 53. That's still too young to retire and old enough to feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, as long as companies don't waste it. I'd push the owners to start retraining, and I'd want a written policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd probably be okay if I use the time. I'd have the kids almost through school and the mortgage down. My real fear is that I'd say 'plenty of time' and not do anything, because that's what I'm like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a yearly review of my own skills and savings, which sounds stiff but I know myself. I'd get proper at using at least one tool. I'd also bring our savings up to six months and talk to Erika about what a smaller house would look like later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a mild way. It's less a fear and more a thing I know I'll have to deal with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know yourself. What would stop you from acting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort. Every year I'd find a reason to wait: the kids' exams, a busy season, a bad quarter. I've done it before with my health, and I'd probably do it again. If I have ten years I'll probably waste the first six of them, because that's how I've always handled things I dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you catch yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Erika to hold me to it, and set one date a year in my diary. It's a bit silly, but if somebody else is watching, I do things. I'd probably tell my boss, too.

say: I'd say ten years is a **decent warning** if companies don't waste it.
I'd push the owners for a **written retraining** policy.
think: I'd probably be okay if I **use the time**.
My real fear is saying **plenty of time** and doing nothing.
do: Set a **yearly review** of my skills and savings.
feel: Mildly **anxious**; something I know I'll have to deal with.
S4.quote: If I have ten years I'll probably waste the first six of them, because that's how I've always handled things I dread.
fieldNote: His threat is **procrastination**, which he admits, not the technology.
He builds **accountability** through Erika and a diary date.
Ten years brings his mood **down** from the other worlds, but not to calm.

steps.text: Review my skills and savings every January with Erika
Get comfortable with one buying tool over two years
Ask the owners for a written retraining policy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'm not fast with change, I know that, and two years gives me no time to catch up. What would help is a company that tells us the truth early, paid training during working hours, and some money to live on while I switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think buyers just place orders. A good buyer is the person a factory calls at midnight when a part breaks, and the machine doesn't have my number. I'd like that to count for something.

headlineQuote: A good buyer is the person a factory calls at midnight when a part breaks, and the machine doesn't have my number.
portrait: David Varga, 43, is **chief buyer** at an industrial supplier, with a wife who manages a dental practice and two school-age children.
Centre in views and **resistant** to change: never uses AI and admits his refusal was partly pride.
Has about **three months** saved and a mortgage, and an owner who may sell, which worries him even in the calm world.
Moves from uneasy to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks, with age 48 as his core fear.
His plan is to **write down** supplier knowledge, learn the tools late, and lean on hands-on work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because he is slow with change and has no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: **Early honesty** from his company and paid training in working hours.
Some **income to live on** while he switches.
